media.title: Joinville Studios — soundstage and lighting grid, 1929
media.description: Interior view of the Société des Cinéromans studios at Joinville-le-Pont, showing the steel roof structure, suspended projectors and overhead lighting equipment. The photograph accompanied Jacques Lefebvre’s industrial report on the Joinville complex in Pour Vous in January 1929.
media.altText: Sepia press photograph of a large film soundstage at Joinville-le-Pont, with steel roof trusses, catwalks and numerous suspended studio lights.
media.publicCaption: Interior of the Cinéromans studios at Joinville-le-Pont, with the overhead lighting grid and suspended projectors, January 1929.

timelineEvents.title: Multiple-language versions and transnational sound-film production
timelineEvents.label: Transnational sound film
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Before 1933, Kaper and Jurmann were already working within the multiple-language version system that linked Babelsberg, Joinville, Vienna, and other European production centres.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The practice of producing parallel language versions was one of the key industrial conditions of early sound cinema. It allowed music to move more easily than dialogue across national markets, even when lyrics, singers, and performance contexts changed. Kaper and Jurmann’s work in this system gave their songs and professional skills a transnational character before their forced departure from Germany.

places.publicNote: Joinville was a French studio and production centre associated with multiple-language versions in early sound cinema.
